pageCache.pageTitle: Welcome back, May Steinberg ’83!  | News Post
pageCache.text:
Welcome back, May Steinberg ’83!
An ASL graduate herself, May recently returned to Waverley Place as our new assistant choral director. We caught up with May to hear what it’s like to come back to return to the School in a whole new role.
What’s a favorite memory from your time at ASL? There are so many of them, but all are centered around those teachers with whom I found ways to connect in some way: science teacher Robert Tener, English teacher Don Jesse, math teacher Paul Fecher, and music teachers Dick and Georgia Bassett. These were the people who inspired me the most, and—particularly the Bassets—molded my path to becoming a music teacher.
What brought you back to teach at ASL? I have always wanted to reconnect with ASL, not necessarily as a lead teacher, but as an accompanist for this amazing music department. The position of assistant choral director was the perfect way for me to reconnect after a successful 38-year career as a lead teacher!
What’s changed since you were a student? The biggest change is the building! When I attended there were only four colored staircases (red, yellow, green, and blue)—and no art building! What’s stayed the same? One thing that hasn't changed is the welcoming feeling I get when I walk through the doors. I feel as happy and content today as I did more than 40 years ago when I was a student. Also, the choir room has not changed, though it was called Music Room A in my day! What do you hope to bring to your students? I hope to share my love of music and the joy that I receive from singing, playing, and making music together!

pageCache.pageTitle: Courageous global citizenship - The American School in London
pageCache.text:
Courageous global citizenship
We are a diverse, international school community in multicultural London. Our mission to empower courageous global citizens commits us to foster knowledge, skills and values that contribute to individual and collective well-being. Through our programs, we grow our global and intercultural competence, helping our students thrive in an interconnected world.

pageCache.pageTitle: Fundamental British values  - The American School in London
pageCache.text:
Fundamental British values at ASL
As an independent day school, providing an exceptional American education to an international student body in the heart of London, we join with our host country in promoting the fundamental British values of democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, and mutual respect and tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs.
As citizens of a vibrant democracy, we fulfill our obligations to ourselves and to others. In our classrooms, innovation and individuality are celebrated, and outstanding academic success is applauded. Students thrive amid the joy of authentic learning experiences. High expectations are clearly communicated and students take ownership of their words and actions. We value diversity of thought and experience and we treat others the way we expect to be treated. Within our school community of more than 65 nationalities and numerous faiths, we express mutual respect and tolerance for those with different beliefs. Committed to creating courageous global citizens, we inspire students to engage with others across lines of difference in a changing world.

pageCache.pageTitle: Inclusivity - The American School in London
pageCache.text:
Inclusivity
We are an independent school offering an American curriculum in England, and we are governed by UK statutory and school inspection requirements along with fundamental British values. We are also guided by our own mission and values as a diverse and international school community.
In the UK, schools are expected to meet the needs of all students and to foster environments where students and adults can connect around their commonalities and work together across their differences. Schools are required to create non-discriminatory cultures where equality and diversity are promoted in alignment with the Equality Act of 2010.
Our diversity, equity and inclusion statement
The American School in London (ASL) is committed to building and sustaining a diverse, equitable and inclusive school community.
Our strength is in our diversity. We are committed to providing equitable access to all facets of school life. ASL is dedicated to fostering an inclusive school environment in which members can thrive and be themselves in a fully authentic manner.
ASL upholds the right to an educational experience in which diverse identities, experiences and ideas are recognized and human dignity is affirmed. Diversity develops better collaborators, braver explorers, stronger communicators, greater innovators and deeper thinkers. From the time children enter the School, they learn to celebrate their differences and similarities, confront stereotypes and biases, and develop an understanding of historical and contemporary struggles and victories in the face of injustice. Through this education, students are empowered to advocate for a more just world and acquire the skills to be courageous global citizens.
Creating a diverse, equitable and inclusive school community is an ever-evolving journey. We challenge ourselves to do this work on a personal and institutional level, with empathy and mutual respect. Building and sustaining a diverse, equitable and inclusive school community is the responsibility of all. Our commitment to diversity, equity and inclusion holds the promise of a better future for all our children.
Equal opportunities policy

pageCache.pageTitle: The American School in London Portrait of a Learner
pageCache.text:
ASL Portrait of a Learner
Our ASL community worked together to identify the traits that exemplify what it is to be a learner at the American School in London. The result of this collaboration is a group of characteristics that are unique to our school.
These essential traits are evident every day at ASL; in our classrooms, at Canons Park, in our hallways, at recess, in the Staff Lounge, on field trips and at school events.
There is a thinker, an explorer, a collaborator, an innovator and a communicator within every student. We care about our well-being, and show respect, responsibility, kindness and integrity in the lives we lead. We value and encourage these characteristics in others. More than anything, we have the courage to act.
Thinker
We use critical and creative thinking skills to analyze ideas and problems. We use inquiry to understand important concepts and questions.
Explorer
We value a sense of wonder and are curious about the world. We cultivate our interests and strengths. We find passion and purpose in our work.
Collaborator
We engage purposefully with others to support common goals. We understand and respect diverse approaches.
Innovator
We seek creative solutions to real-life problems. We value mistakes as learning opportunities.
Communicator
We listen, speak and write effectively. We communicate clearly with others through dialogue and participation. We value the ability to do so in multiple languages. We attend to the perspectives of other individuals and groups.
Well-being
We seek a balance of mind, body and spirit as we grow. We are conscious of our health in the choices we make.
Respect
We treat others the way we expect to be treated. We appreciate our own cultures and personal histories. We value diversity of thought and experience.
Responsibility
We take ownership of our words, actions and learning. We fulfill our obligations to ourselves and to others.
Kindness
We act with compassion. We help others.
Integrity
We are honest. We work hard. We make the right choice even when no one is watching.
Courage to Act
We stretch and grow by taking risks. We are resourceful in the face of challenges and change. We have the courage to speak up for ourselves and for others. We take positive action to make our community and world a better place.

pageCache.pageTitle: Farewell to our 2026 leavers | News Post
pageCache.text:
Farewell to our 2026 leavers
As the academic year draws to a close, we want to express our deepest gratitude to ASL’s departing employees. This list honors those who moved on to next chapters earlier in the 2025–26 school year, as well as those leaving us this month. Each of these individuals has made a wonderful impact on our community, and the School is far better for it. Thank you, 2026 leavers, for your years of dedicated service to the ASL community!
Sue Moffat (ASL 1992–2026), administrative assistant to the lower school principal “Sue has been the heartbeat of the Lower School for 34 extraordinary years. Through four lower school principals, six assistant principals, and six heads of school—and a jaw-dropping 100-plus-mile round trip commute—Sue has been the steady, brilliant presence that keeps everything running. Need an answer to an impossible question? Sue had it. Need a laugh on a tough day? Sue delivered, often from her desk, where her infectious humor brightened everyone’s spirits. And then there are the cards—those beautiful, hand-crafted birthday cards that Sue created with such care. Colleagues from across ASL would make the pilgrimage to the Lower School Office not just for a card, but for the personal touch and love Sue poured into each one. Sue has been the anchor we could always rely on, the colleague who knows everyone, the friend who made us smile, and the irreplaceable voice of the lower school community. We’re already missing her, and we’ll continue to miss her deeply. But Sue’s legacy at ASL—especially in the Lower School—is permanent. Once an Eagle, always an Eagle!” – Sarah Ong (ASL 1994–present), Sacha McVean (ASL 2017–present), and Patrick Lee (ASL 1995–98, 2002–present)
Helen Jackson ’79 P ’23 (ASL 1994–2026), psychologist “Helen’s combination of brilliance and humility is exactly why she is the heart and soul of ASL. Her history here goes all the way back to her own days as an ASL student, and has continued far beyond for the last 31 years. When our SLD program was in its infancy, Helen was there to lay the building blocks we still use today. Helen knew the ‘before,’ and for more than three decades, she shaped the ‘after.’ From creating our database to drafting handbooks whose structures still guide us today, Helen has been an irreplaceable pillar of our student support ecosystem. She will be surely missed by all!” – Leah Duggan P ’36 ’38 (ASL 2012–present), Jo Shearer P ’30 ’32 (ASL 2020–present), Yanna Jackson (ASL 2023–present), and Heather Statz P ’36 (ASL 2017–present)
Frank Sousa (ASL 2006–26), high school math teacher “Frank will be missed dearly in the high school math department. In addition to being a dedicated teacher, he is the brainpower behind all logistics in our department. That’s part of who Frank is. He is a problem-solver. He's the dry wit that makes you laugh when you least expect it. He is the colleague who is warm without being overly sentimental. He is witty without being unkind, and he is present without ever demanding attention.
Frank’s superpower is his ability to create connections. He has built professional friendships that span six countries and four continents. Wherever Frank goes, he finds his people. More importantly, he keeps them—and every single one of them would tell you the exact same thing: Frank has this gift for making you feel like you belong in his life. Permanently.”
— Peggy Stetsko (ASL 2017–present), Jenny Wexler (ASL 2015–17, 2019–present), and Patrick Lee (ASL 1995–98, 2002–present)
Ania Driscoll-Lind P ’10 ’13 (ASL 2007–present), lower school environmental education teacher “Ania brings her passion for science and the natural world to all of her interactions with lower school children. She has a wonderful ability to nurture curiosity, encouraging pupils to ask questions, investigate, and discover through hands-on experiences. Whether she is walking the hedgerow at Canons Park, or looking under logs or in the willow tunnels, she shows the children how to look closely and connect with the cycles of growth, rest, and renewal. Ania encouraged us to slow down, to notice, to ask questions, and to wonder. She is a collaborative colleague who worked with lower school teachers to provide the best opportunities for all students to engage meaningfully in science, the natural world, and the art of traditional willow making. Her creativity, patience, and genuine love of teaching help every child to feel valued and excited about learning, leaving a lasting impression on both her pupils and those fortunate enough to work alongside her.”
– Melanie O’Leary P ’11 (ASL 1997–99, 2003–present)
Sean Ross P ’20 (ASL 2009–26), middle school community action integrationist “Sean is an incredible educator and person, and he embodies the ASL community action motto of ’heads, heart, and hands.’ He has a rare gift for helping students engage with complex social justice issues, and creating spaces where every voice is valued and heard. Whether leading the Global Issues & Community Action class, supporting community partners, packing food parcels, or shepherding grandfriends, Sean consistently turns values into action. He is a great thinker and strategist, but above all, he is driven by a deep care for people. His kindness, empathy, and unwavering commitment to others have strengthened countless relationships across ASL and beyond. Sean leaves a lasting legacy of compassion, service, and connection, and our community is richer for having learned alongside him.”
— Brandon Block P ’29 (ASL 2014–present)
Whitney Nuchereno (ASL 2012–26), high school world languages and cultures teacher
“I have known Whitney for a long time—since 2009, to be precise, when we were studying for our master’s degrees at Middlebury’s School of French in Paris. Whitney’s passion for languages and for helping others learn was palpable, so it was no surprise that we ended up as department colleagues at ASL just three years later. Whether it was dreaming up exciting activities for our students, leading training workshops for other professionals here at ASL and at the national ACTFL convention, coaching tennis, advising the National Honor Society, or creating engaging cultural itineraries for students on Alternatives, Whitney has given her heart and soul to ASL. We will miss her very much and wish her all the best in her new career in wine back in the United States, where her enthusiasm for teaching and learning will surely take her far!”
— Mario Rojas Acosta (ASL 2011–21; 2021–present)
John Farmer ’97 P ’29 ’31 (ASL 2012–26), director of athletics
“John’s passion for ASL and our athletics program has left an indelible mark on our students, staff, and the entire community. It is no exaggeration to say that John bleeds orange and black. On any given day, he was every student-athlete’s biggest cheerleader and fiercest advocate, both on and off the court.
What truly defined John was his heart. He was the kind of leader who always wanted to hear about you first, whether it was a quick update on how you were doing, or eagerly asking, ’How did Arsenal, Duke, or the 49ers do?’ Looking back, those everyday conversations are what I will miss the most.
John, thank you for your unwavering dedication, support, and the deep care you showed to everyone around you. You leave behind a legacy that will inspire us all.”
— Ryan Erickson (ASL 2020–present)
Steve Reed (ASL 2012–26), library administrative assistant
“Steve was the heart and soul of the Mellon Library for 14 years. When I started working in the library five years ago, he welcomed me with warmth, as if we had known each other for ages. Despite his humility, he possessed an incredible breadth of knowledge about books. He rarely let any student or adult leave without saying, ’Oh, wait! What about this one?’ He would then recommend an obscure book with a terrible cover that the reader would end up devouring. Steve is already sorely missed, and the library is better for having had him as a strong presence during all those years.”
— Staci Fox P ’35 ’38 (ASL 2021–present)
Patricia Elsea (ASL 2016–26), middle school english as an additional language (EAL) teacher
“Patricia is passionate about teaching multilingual students and acting as a tireless advocate for maintaining home languages—and she always delights in opportunities to converse in Spanish. Beyond the classroom, she is never one to shy away from a variety of responsibilities; she models genuine interest and enthusiasm for every task she takes on. Her approach to education is grounded in a deep sense of justice, as she consistently strives to meet the unique needs of all her students. We will miss her many passions—from Model UN to gardening; from travel to theater—not to mention her stylish outfits. We wish her all the best in her future adventures.
– Nanette Pakula P ’12 ’15 ’16 ’20 ASL (2007–present) and Darryl Phelps (ASL 1998–2025)
Shrita Gajendragadkar (ASL 2016–26), high school social studies teacher “To me, Shrita has been the best colleague I could ever wish for. She has been a model teacher who always puts student learning at the center of her work; an authentic intellect who challenges me to think more carefully, without preconceived ideas; and above all, a true friend with whom I can share the joys, sorrows, and everything in between. I will miss her dearly.”
— Lanting Xu (ASL 2011–present)
Anne Richardson (ASL 2017–26), director of the office of student advising; university advisor
“Anne has served ASL extraordinarily well during her time at ASL. Her portfolio of responsibilities is wide and seemed to grow every year—yet she always centered students in every decision she made. She is a servant leader, anticipating the needs of her team, supporting them every step along the way, and providing homemade baked goods at critical moments in the school year. Anne has provided sage wisdom, critical insight, and loving care to hundreds of ASL students and families as they navigated the post-ASL planning and application process, helping them to focus on finding the ‘just right’ fit for them. The consummate team player, Anne does it all, and with healthy doses of wit, good humor, and infectious laughter. We will miss her terribly, but the legacy of her loving presence will live on in the halls of ASL for years to come.”
– Catherine Ezzo P ’28 (ASL 2025–present)
Grace Kasangila P ’26 ’26 (ASL 2016–26), registrar “To say Grace will be missed is an understatement. To say we’ll be okay next year without her is a lie. Grace is the kind of person that brings levity to your day when you’re down, she stands in your corner helping you navigate life’s ups and downs, and she’ll pull you up when you’re doing wrong. She brings warmth, laughter, and a welcoming presence to OSA, making it feel less like an office and more like a family.
When I started at ASL seven years ago, I never imagined I would find one of my closest friends. I’m going to miss our morning meetings, our constant interruptions while trying to work, our laughs, our tears, and all the moments that have become such an important part of my daily routine. ASL won’t be the same without her.”
– Terri Okpoyo P ’23 ’23 ’33 (ASL 2019–present)
Sandrine Wright (ASL 2020–26), grade 3 teacher “Sandrine swept into ASL as a substitute ready for anything. A modern-day Mary Poppins, with her bag of tricks and a supercalifragilistic personality. Her infectious laughter soon filled our hallways, and her ’can-do’ attitude led to her current role as a lead teacher in Grade 3. We will be forever grateful to have worked alongside Sandrine, and we will always miss her spark of energy, her natural ability to face challenges with diplomacy, her passion for literacy, and her absolute love of being a teacher and spending her days surrounded by children.” — Sacha McVean (ASL 2017–present)
Wendy Robinson (ASL 1992–2026), director of publications & copywriting “We have so much to thank Wendy for—her unfailing positivity and kindness always made working alongside her a delight. We also appreciate her scrupulous approach to written communication, as well as her meticulous editing. Wendy has made many contributions to ASL over the years—in college counselling, admissions, communications and advancement. She is eager to help and is beloved among the ASL community. We remark on her integrity, her extraordinary professionalism, warmed with her friendship, and the generous spirit she brought to everything she did. Wendy draws people in, and she had an enormous impact on those lucky enough to know her—students, parents, employees and alumni. Incredibly funny, quick-witted, perceptive and trusted, she has epitomized the best of ASL. Her sense of humor is legendary and so is her kind and benevolent heart. For so many, her guidance, knowledge and hilarious commentary will be sorely missed. Wendy should be bursting with pride from all she has contributed to ASL.” —Compiled by Katherine Precht P ’08 ’15 (ASL 1993-2012) and Jodi Warren (ASL 1988-2023)

pageCache.pageTitle: 75 years of… ASL field trips! | News Post
pageCache.text:
75 years of… ASL field trips!
This is the first in our series looking back at 75 years of ASL. We’ve grown, moved, and changed quite a bit since 1951, but some things—like ASL’s commitment to building global citizens, in part through travel around London, the UK, and the wider world—have stayed the same! In this story, we’ll take a peek back in time at just a few of the thousands of memorable field trips that have made ASL special over the past three-quarters of a century. For more ASL history, please visit our brand new online timeline!
The American School in London carries a sense of movement in its name—and from its very inception in the early 1950s, movement has been a cornerstone of an ASL education. “Tours to places of historical, cultural and scientific interest are a regular feature of the curriculum. Students are given every chance to witness occasions of national interest as well as historical locations and museums,” ASL’s founding headmaster, Stephen L. Eckard (ASL 1951–71), once said of the earliest Eagles’ experience of the School.
ASL students visit a London ice cream factory in the 1950s.
In 2005, Tim Blick ’64 recalled fond memories of attending ASL in the late 1950s: “As a class, we would journey out every Wednesday morning to see some new part of English history, be it the planetarium, Madame Tussaud’s, or the British Museum. We would always sit upstairs on the double-decker bus and return just before 3 pm.”
These Wednesday field trips were, in fact, a school-wide requirement during ASL’s early days—but field trips could also (and often did!) happen outside of these mid-week excursions, and they weren’t always strictly educational.
In the 1960 all-school yearbook—ASL’s first!—high school student editors wrote, “As Christmas [1959] drew near, the seniors retired to Hampshire for a day of Christmas tree chopping directed by the chief of the tribe, Mr. Eckard. This was carried out on a magnificent level in brilliant drizzle with ensuing sniffles and sore muscles. The booty was brought back by truck and the seniors in a baggage car accompanied by Her Majesty’s soldiers.”
Grade 5 students, meanwhile, recalled in that same yearbook their own 1959–60 trips to London’s Science Museum, Natural History Museum, and Kensington Palace, and looked forward to an upcoming visit to the ZSL London Zoo, while Grades 1 and 2 discussed zoo trips aplenty, and the many underwater creatures they had seen on an aquarium visit.
In 1974, Music Tour took place for the first time, with ASL’s stage band visiting The Hague for their inaugural overseas trip. In 2026—52 years later!—ASL’s high school band visited The Hague on Music Tour once again, playing a warehouse venue in addition to a joint performance with the American School of the Hague. (At the same time, ASL’s other high school musicians—specifically our orchestra and choir groups!—headed to Norfolk and Cardiff, respectively, for their own 2026 Music Tour experiences.)
The Hague, like so many European destinations, has also played host to countless other ASL field trips, including International School Sports Tournament (ISST) athletics competitions, and quite a few Model United Nations conferences, too. Former high school history teacher John Wilson (ASL 1971–2009) was key in championing the School’s Model UN program as soon as he joined ASL, and took many a delegation across the Channel for days-long experiments in international cooperation.
An ASL delegation representing the Soviet Union appears at a 1972 Model United Nations conference.
In 1978, as an “alternative” to the Music Tour that high school musicians were, by that point, taking every year, a new tradition was born in the High School: Alternatives. The trips, which quickly became an ASL institution, are generally four days long, and have taken multi-grade groups of students everywhere from Russia to the Canary Islands to Iceland to Cyprus; all across the UK, France, Spain, Italy, Scandinavia, the Balkans—and beyond.
1988 yearbook editors introduced a long spread of Alternatives photos and quips by excerpting a letter sent around the High School that year by Clayton Lewis P ’01 ’03 (ASL 1980–94), the divisional principal at the time, which said that the program had two main goals. The first, Mr. Lewis wrote, was to “enrich the quality of our curricular and extracurricular program by providing a wide range of educational, cultural, and recreational activities.” The second aim of Alternatives was, in his words, “the socialization process, one that brings together seemingly disparate students (new-returning, younger-older, extrovert-introvert) into close and meaningful associations.”
Even beyond the ASL student body, Alternatives—like many other ASL field trips over the decades—have long built bridges and mutual understanding.
In 1979, the high school yearbook reported, history teacher Steve McCollum (ASL 1975–79) launched an exchange program between ASL and a school in Cologne after speaking with a teacher at the German school that Alternatives travelers had visited the year prior. “In the autumn, the German students visited ASL for a week,” the yearbook reported. “ASL students repaid the compliment by visiting with the Germans, judging that the Germans had been friendlier and more helpful than we had been, perhaps because most of them spoke English and few of us spoke German.”
“As they return from their respective adventures,” high school Principal Lewis continued in the 1988 yearbook, “the barriers that divide or isolate students are to a large degree lifted.”
That same year, the Quoi de Neuf (the former name of the Scroll, ASL’s still-thriving middle school student newspaper) ran a series of articles recapping weeklong middle school trips around the UK and Europe, with groups travelling around Greece—where Grade 6 students toured Athens, Crete, Delphi, and Mycenae, and performed a play by Aristophanes in Epidaurus—as well as Wales, Holland, and Dorset.
Grade 4 students enjoy the 2025 Bushcraft trip.
This year’s Grade 6 students will pick between trips to Isle of Wight, the Peak District, North Wales, Hadrian’s Wall, and bath, while Grade 5 heads to the English coastal village of Calshot, Grade 7 goes to Dublin, and Grade 8 will take their traditional annual trip to the beaches of Normandy to study WWII history.
Grade 4, preparing to enter middle school, also takes advantage of spring weather with a formative two-night tradition of their own: the whole grade travels to Bushcraft, an outdoor education center in Cambridge where they live and work within trip-specific “tribes,” which mix classes and encourage whole-grade bonding. They sleep outdoors, and learn essential outdoors skills such as outdoor cooking, fire-building, wilderness first aid, and more—while also doing activities like axe-throwing, archery, whittling, and building shelter.
The Bushcraft trip, now approaching 10 years old, replaced Grade 4’s earlier Canada Coombe overnight tradition, and really is “proper camping,” reports Sarah Ong (ASL 1994-present), lower school administrative assistant and trip organizer for the past five years. “It’s dark, and there’s no electricity.” Bushcraft is well loved by students—even if, for many of those heading away from home for the first time, it can inspire some anxiety ahead of time.
“More than anything, we get a sense of community,” says Grade 4 teacher Elliott Green (ASL 2018-present) of Bushcraft. “It’s a lovely time for students to culminate their time in the Lower School. You see independence, the courage to act, bravery, and kids getting messy—and not taking themselves too seriously.
From double-decker buses in 1950s London to performances in The Hague and nights under the stars in Cambridge, ASL field trips have always been about more than travel. They are about curiosity, connection, and growth—about stepping beyond the classroom and into the wider world. 75 years on, that spirit of movement continues to define an ASL education.

High School community partnerships
ASL provides students with many opportunities to take action in our community, helping students gain deeper understanding of our local and global communities, and discover new aspects of themselves, the skills they offer, and the impact they can have.
Community partnerships are the core of our high school program. The partnerships give students the opportunity to work after school directly with people from the broader London community. Programs take place in a variety of settings—including youth centers, schools, playgrounds, shelters, and senior citizen centers—and give students the chance to work with people in a wide range of circumstances.
The community partnerships program is aligned with our athletic seasons. Partnerships take place once a week after school for two hours. Students travel to and from the partnership as a group along with their partnership coach (an ASL faculty/staff member). Students commit to one season at a time.
As with all high school commitments, we take attendance seriously. Students with repeated or unexcused absences are asked to step down from the program.
At the end of each semester, advisors, deans and college counselor receive an assessment of their students’ performance in the program, which they may share with parents and students.
After registration, parents will be emailed a link to an online consent form which they will be asked to submit before the first meeting of the season.
Students are accompanied to each site by a member of staff. Depending on the site location, students will walk, take a bus or school van, or underground train to the site. Students are then invited to return to ASL with a teacher or in ASL approved transport, or, with parental consent, are permitted to make their own way home directly from the site.
After school on the first day of each season, an orientation meeting takes place in O-320, O-321 and O-322 in the High School.
Group reflection is a key part of the learning associated with the program. It is integrated into the daily sessions by coaches.
Community partnerships follow the school athletic season calendar. Students register for one athletic season at a time, enabling them to alternate between partnerships and sports participation.

Adventure Play Hub offers popular after-school programs for local primary-age children, with indoor spaces for arts, crafts, music and table tennis and outdoor areas for basketball, gardening and play.
ASL students participate in sessions led by Adventure Play Hub staff, building relationships with younger children and joining arts, sports and play activities. Students also help with snacks and contribute to creating a welcoming and inclusive environment.
Through sustained participation, students develop communication and relationship-building skills and begin to understand how play, consistency and welcoming community spaces can support children’s sense of belonging.
Learn more about Adventure Play Hub.
Barrow Hill Junior School is located nearby in St John’s Wood. Through Dance Squad, ASL students work with ASL staff to design activities for an after-school dance experience for children aged 7–10, with Barrow Hill staff providing oversight of the program.
Students interested in dance, movement and working with younger children have the opportunity to help plan activities, build relationships with participants and contribute to sessions over the course of the season.
In doing so, students develop collaborative planning, communication, responsiveness and age-appropriate leadership, learning how to adapt activities for younger participants and work responsibly within a partner-school setting.
With the graduation of previous student leaders, we are currently looking for students interested in helping develop the next phase of the program. If interested, please contact Mr. Block.
Doorstep supports families living in temporary accommodation after losing their homes.
As part of this partnership, ASL students spend time in Doorstep’s after-school program alongside Doorstep staff and an ASL coach. Students build relationships with children through games, arts and crafts, conversation and homework support, while contributing to the welcoming environment of the program.
Before and throughout the partnership, students learn about homelessness, housing insecurity and the experiences of families living in temporary accommodation. Regular reflection helps students connect what they observe at Doorstep with wider questions of inequality, belonging, stability and community support.
Along the way, students develop empathy, communication, safeguarding awareness and reflective skills while deepening their understanding of how housing insecurity can affect children and families and how community organizations provide consistency, connection and support.
Want to learn more about how young children develop, communicate and build relationships?
Through The Winch’s SPLAT program at England’s Lane, ASL students spend time alongside staff and families in a program for toddlers and young children. Students participate in play and age-appropriate activities within the staff-led program.
Students develop observation, communication and age-appropriate interaction skills while learning more about early childhood development and the role of supportive community spaces for families.
This is a limited opportunity particularly suited to students with a strong interest in child development and working with younger children. If interested, please contact Mr. Block.
PACE runs after-school youth programs at sites in Fortune Green and Camden. Its centers provide welcoming spaces where young people can spend time with friends, take part in arts and creative activities, play football and enjoy outdoor play.
ASL students visit weekly alongside their ASL coach and PACE staff, taking part in the life of the youth club by building relationships, joining games and activities, noticing how staff create an inclusive and supportive environment, and contributing where helpful.
Throughout the season, students use short topic and reflection activities to explore issues including local inequality, food insecurity, belonging, safe community spaces, stability, friendship, identity, neurodiversity, play and mental-health access.
This gives students a structured way to develop observation, reflection, communication and relationship-building skills while considering how youth organizations create belonging, stability and opportunity and how wider social and economic conditions shape young people’s experiences.
The Homework Buddy program creates a sustained peer relationship between High School and Middle School students at ASL.
High School students are paired with Middle School students and meet once a week in the library over several months. During these sessions, High School students support younger students with organization, homework and academic routines while developing their own skills in communication, patience and responsible peer leadership.
The emphasis is not simply on completing homework, but on building a consistent and supportive relationship that helps younger students develop confidence and effective learning habits.
High School students develop communication, patience, reliability and reflective peer-leadership skills as they learn how to support another student without taking over.
Some of our most exciting after-school partnerships grow from student interests, ideas and commitment. In recent years, students have helped develop collaborative projects involving dance, robotics, sustainability, art and other shared activities with local schools and community organisations. Student-designed partnerships are developed in collaboration with Community Action staff and our partner organisations, with appropriate adult oversight and safeguarding arrangements in place. They are intended to create opportunities for shared learning, connection and meaningful engagement with the wider community. If you have an idea for a partnership you would like to explore, reach out to Brandon Block.
Explore how robotics can become a tool for collaboration, problem-solving and connection with younger students.
ASL students first meet at school to develop the robotics knowledge, activity-planning skills and safeguarding awareness they will need for the partnership. They then take part in staff-supervised sessions at local primary schools, supporting Grade 4 and 5 students as they design and build robots.
ASL students help younger participants experiment, solve problems and work collaboratively rather than simply providing answers.
In the process, students develop communication, technical explanation, collaborative problem-solving and responsible leadership skills while reflecting on how educational opportunities and expertise can be shared across school communities.
No previous robotics experience is required; preparation is built into the program.
Rugby Portobello Trust is a youth organization that provides educational and recreational opportunities for children and young people in West London. Its after-school program combines academic support with opportunities for play, creativity and relationship-building.
ASL students participate weekly alongside Rugby Portobello staff and their ASL coach. The sustained nature of the partnership allows students to build relationships with younger participants while learning about educational opportunity, youth provision and the importance of reliable community spaces.

Tuesday program
Students work alongside staff to provide homework and learning support for children aged 8–12. The aim is to encourage confidence, persistence and positive learning habits rather than simply completing work for students. After the academic portion of the session, ASL students join participants in recreational activities and games.
Wednesday program
Students support younger children aged 6–8 with age-appropriate learning activities alongside Rugby Portobello staff. They may also help plan and facilitate cultural, creative or recreational activities as part of the wider program.
Across both programs, ASL students reflect on the relationships they develop, the different educational opportunities available to young people and the role sustained community organizations can play in supporting children and families. They also develop patience, communication, reliability and age-appropriate leadership through sustained participation.
The Winch is a youth organization in Swiss Cottage that provides activities, relationships and support for children and families in the local community.
ASL students participate in The Winch’s after-school program alongside Winch staff and their ASL coach. Sessions may include games, arts and crafts, conversation and homework support. Students build sustained relationships with children while learning about the role youth organizations play in creating safe, inclusive and supportive community spaces.
Students with a particular interest or skill may also work with Winch staff and their ASL coach to develop an appropriate small-group activity, such as drama or another creative project. Any such activity is planned collaboratively with the partner and forms part of the wider supervised program.
Students develop communication, adaptability, safeguarding awareness and relationship-building skills while learning how youth organizations create belonging, consistency and opportunity for children and families.
The Winch is lively, creative and energetic, so this partnership is particularly well suited to students who enjoy busy environments and engaging with younger children.
Xcelero Coding Club grew from ASL students’ interest in computer science and educational opportunity. The partnership connects ASL students with young people at Harris Academy St John’s Wood through a weekly coding program.
ASL students participate in staff-supervised sessions, supporting participants as they explore programming, problem-solving and computational thinking.
Students develop technical communication, collaborative problem-solving and responsible leadership skills while helping make computer science learning engaging and accessible to younger participants.
youngPOWER is ASL’s annual student diversity and dialogue conference, developed in partnership with young people from Westminster Academy.
Students serving on the Executive Team and Project Board work collaboratively with ASL staff and partner-school students to shape the conference. They help develop themes, activities and opportunities for dialogue and reflection, while learning about identity, perspective, inclusion and responsible leadership.
